summary: Defines LDP, the Label Distribution Protocol, which lets MPLS routers tell each other which labels they have assigned to which traffic. Without this agreement, labels would have no shared meaning. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5036.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS forwards packets using short labels instead of addresses. Every router on the path replaces the label on a packet with a new one for the next hop, so all of them have to agree on what the labels mean. LDP is the protocol they use to make that agreement, by telling each other which label they have assigned to which traffic.

subtitle: The protocol MPLS routers use to agree on what each label means.

tldr.problem: In MPLS a packet carries a short label that each router swaps for another as the packet moves along the path. That only works if every router on the path agrees on what each label means, and no such agreement existed.
tldr.mechanism: LDP is a set of procedures and messages by which routers exchange label bindings. Discovery uses UDP Hellos, sessions and label exchange use TCP, and four kinds of message cover discovery, sessions, advertisements and notifications.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3036 is a Proposed Standard from January 2001 and has been obsoleted by RFC 5036, which restates the LDP specification.

facts.label: LDP identifier
facts.value: Six octets: four for the router, two for the label space

facts.label: Initialization retry delay
facts.value: At least 15 seconds, growing to at least 2 minutes

today: RFC 3036 is a Proposed Standard from January 2001, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5036, which restates the LDP specification. The RFC itself notes that the MPLS architecture does not assume a single label distribution protocol, and that several were being standardised.

sections.title: Why Labels Need a Protocol
sections.content:
In MPLS, a packet does not carry a destination address at each hop. It carries a short label, and each router swaps that label for another one as it forwards the packet. For that to work, the routers along the path have to agree on what each label means, and the label a router sends downstream must mean the same thing to the router that receives it.

This RFC defines LDP, the Label Distribution Protocol, the set of procedures and messages by which routers tell each other which labels they have assigned. Without such an agreement a label has no shared meaning and the path cannot be built.

Four kinds of message do the work. Discovery messages announce and maintain the presence of a router. Session messages establish, maintain and terminate the relationship between two peers. Advertisement messages create, change and delete label bindings for forwarding equivalence classes. Notification messages carry advisory information and signal errors. The Hello message is sent over UDP to the all-routers-on-this-subnet multicast address; everything else travels over TCP, because label distribution needs reliable and in-order delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is only useful if the routers on both sides of a link read it the same way. LDP is the conversation in which they agree, and it runs over TCP so that nothing is lost or reordered on the way.

sections.title: FECs and How Packets Find Their Path
sections.content:
A forwarding equivalence class is the set of IP packets that may travel along a given label switched path. Each FEC is described by one or more FEC elements. Two are defined: an address prefix, of any length from zero to a full address, and a host address, which is a full address.

The rules for choosing a path for a packet are applied in turn. If exactly one path has a host address element identical to the packet's destination address, the packet goes there. Failing that, if the packet matches exactly one path it goes there; if it matches several, it goes to the one whose matching prefix is longest. An address prefix element that names a full address is not the same thing as a host address element with the same address, and the host address always wins.

Each router keeps the labels it has learned in a Label Information Base. When the next hop for a prefix changes, the router has to find the label the new next hop advertised, which means mapping an address to the peer's LDP identifier. To make that possible, routers advertise their own addresses with Address messages and withdraw them with Address Withdraw messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label switched path is described by the traffic it carries: either a prefix such as a network address, or one exact host address. A packet goes to the path with the longest prefix that covers its destination, and an exact host match always beats a prefix match.

sections.title: Discovery and Session Establishment
sections.content:
Discovery removes the need to configure label switching peers by hand. In the basic mechanism a router sends Link Hellos out an interface as UDP packets to the all-routers-on-this-subnet group address; receiving one creates a hello adjacency with a potential peer and tells the router which label space the peer intends to use. In the extended mechanism a router sends Targeted Hellos to one specific address, which finds routers that are not directly connected. Extended discovery is asymmetric: the initiator sends, and the targeted router decides whether to answer with its own Targeted Hellos.

Once two routers have exchanged Hellos they establish a session in two steps: a transport connection, then session initialization. The active side opens a TCP connection and sends an Initialization message. The passive side matches the LDP identifier in that message against the hello adjacencies it has, checks that the proposed session parameters are acceptable, and answers with its own Initialization message and a KeepAlive. A KeepAlive then completes the exchange for the active side.

The parameters negotiated include the protocol version, the label distribution method, timer values, and the VPI and VCI ranges for label controlled ATM and the DLCI ranges for label controlled Frame Relay. If the parameters are unacceptable the passive side sends a Session Rejected error notification and closes the connection; if it cannot find a matching hello adjacency it sends a No Hello error notification and closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Two steps happen before any label is exchanged. First the routers find each other by shouting a Hello onto the network, and then they agree on how to talk to each other over a TCP connection. Each side has a role, and the two messages that carry the agreement are an Initialization and a KeepAlive.

sections.title: The Session Initialization State Machine
sections.content:
The RFC describes session negotiation as a state machine with five states. A session starts as NON EXISTENT and moves to INITIALIZED when the TCP connection is established. The active role then transmits an Initialization message and moves to OPENSENT; the passive role moves to OPENREC when it receives an acceptable Initialization message, sending its own Initialization message and a KeepAlive in reply.

From OPENREC, a KeepAlive moves the session to OPERATIONAL. From OPENSENT, an acceptable Initialization message moves it to OPENREC and a KeepAlive is sent back. Receiving any message other than an Initialization message in any of the first four states is an error: the router transmits an error notification and closes the transport connection, returning to NON EXISTENT. From OPERATIONAL, a Shutdown message or a timeout ends the session the same way.

The RFC also warns about a failure mode. Two routers configured incompatibly can each reject the other's Initialization message and keep rejecting it forever. To prevent that, a router must delay its next attempt to open the transport connection by at least 15 seconds after a rejection, with the delay growing to at least two minutes, and it is recommended that an operator be told.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC turns the handshake into five named states with a table of what may happen in each. The table matters because it says what to do with every message that arrives: anything unexpected in the early states ends the session and produces an error notification.

sections.title: Distributing and Managing Labels
sections.content:
Two label distribution methods are defined. With Downstream on Demand, a router hands out a label binding only when a neighbour asks for it with a Label Request. With Downstream Unsolicited, it advertises bindings to its neighbours without being asked, whenever it is ready to switch that traffic. Each interface is configured for one method or the other, and the two routers exchange their choice during initialization.

Two control modes govern the order of events. Under independent control each router may advertise at any time, so an upstream label can be sent before the downstream label has arrived. Under ordered control a router may only pass a label upstream once it holds the label for the next hop, or it is itself the egress. A router is the egress for a FEC when the FEC refers to the router, when the next hop is outside the label switching network, or when the FEC crosses a routing domain boundary.

Two retention modes decide what a router does with a label it learned from a peer that is not its next hop. Conservative retention keeps only labels that will be used for forwarding, which suits devices with little label space but needs a fresh label after a routing change. Liberal retention keeps every label learned, so a routing change can be acted on quickly, at the cost of holding labels that are not needed.

Loop detection is an optional mechanism built on two fields that travel in Label Request and Label Mapping messages. A Path Vector lists the routers the message has crossed; a router that finds its own identifier in the list concludes the message has looped. A Hop Count counts the routers crossed, and reaching the configured maximum is treated the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two choices to make about labels. Should a router hand one out only when asked, or offer it unasked? And should it wait for the label from the next hop before passing one upstream, or announce straight away? Both answers are in the RFC, along with a rule for how much labelling state a router keeps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LDP has two kinds of communication that can be spoofed. Discovery over UDP can be attacked by sending false Hello messages; the RFC's advice is to accept Basic Hellos only on interfaces where trusted routers are directly connected, to ignore Basic Hellos not addressed to the all-routers multicast group, and to filter Targeted Hellos against an access list. Session traffic over TCP can be protected with the TCP MD5 Signature Option, which LDP specifies for the authenticity and integrity of session messages. The RFC notes that MD5 is considered too weak by some, and that LDP could move to a stronger digest once one is defined.

LDP offers no privacy for label distribution. The RFC argues that privacy would not help against label spoofing anyway, since data packets carry their labels in the clear, and that the real defence is to ensure that only trusted routers label packets and that the labels they use were properly learned.

Denial of service is the third area. The well-known UDP discovery port can be flooded, and the RFC's advice is to connect only to peers that can be trusted not to do it, and to filter Targeted Hellos with access lists. At the edge of a trusted MPLS cloud, that filtering can be done once, protecting the routers inside at the cost of the routers at the edge.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the network could send a false Hello and pretend to be a router. The RFC's answer is to restrict who may send Hellos, and to protect the TCP session with the TCP MD5 signature option so that the label exchanges cannot be tampered with.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Two octet unsigned integer holding the protocol version. This document specifies version 1.

fields.name: PDU Length
fields.desc: Total length of the PDU in octets, excluding the Version and PDU Length fields. The maximum is negotiable at session setup; before that it is 4096 bytes.

fields.name: LDP Identifier
fields.desc: Six octets identifying the label space of the sending router. The first four octets identify the router and must be globally unique; the last two identify a label space within it.

viz.caption: THE FOUR KINDS OF LDP MESSAGE (RFC 3036)

items.title: Discovery
items.text: Announce and maintain the presence of a router in the network. The Hello message is sent over UDP to the all-routers-on-this-subnet group address.

items.title: Session
items.text: Establish, maintain and terminate sessions between LDP peers, over TCP.

items.title: Advertisement
items.text: Create, change and delete label mappings for FECs, over TCP.

items.title: Notification
items.text: Provide advisory information and signal error information. An error notification closes the session.
